title: Cognitive Reclamation and Acceleration: Why We Built DebatingAI (Literacy)
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard and Dr. Anand Rao, founders of DebatingAI, argue that AI has created a cognitive offloading crisis in education and that debate — specifically competitive switch-side debate — is the most ready-to-deploy pedagogical response. The article opens with the founders' shared history as high school and college debaters turned educators and argues that AI is disrupting education faster than most are willing to admit. Schools have responded in three inadequate ways: doing nothing, banning AI, or deploying chatbots on top of unreformed curricula. Bauschard argues all three fail because they do not address the fundamental redesign problem: assessment and instruction must shift toward activities that AI cannot do for students — building judgment, demanding defense, rewarding original thinking under pressure. Debate is presented as uniquely suited to this challenge because it requires students to understand positions they oppose, adapt in real time to a live opponent, and defend claims without a chatbot intermediary. The article quotes Sam Altman warning about critical thinking atrophy if instruction does not change.
points: AI is not a future threat to education — it is already inside the classroom, and the cognitive offloading it enables is measurable. Fluent use of AI tools is not skilled use; the gap between the two is wider for AI than for any prior technology.

All three mainstream school responses — ignore, ban, or deploy — fail to address the core problem: if assessment still depends on outputs AI can generate, no policy on access changes whether students are actually thinking.

Debate is the most ready-to-go response because it puts the human back at the center: facing a live opponent demands judgment, adaptation, and listening that AI cannot offload. Switch-side debate forces genuine comprehension of opposed positions, a level of understanding no one-sided AI-assisted essay produces.

Sam Altman's Stanford CS 153 warning provides the article's urgency: 'If we continue to teach and evaluate students as if we were in a pre-AGI world, it's not going to work and it is going to lead to atrophy of learning how to think.'

Banning AI fails because AI is now a cognitive layer — ubiquitous across devices students carry — and banning it from school while students use it at home creates a class divide and produces students excluded from the world AI is building.
quotes: We'll say the quiet part out loud: AI is changing the world faster than most people are willing to admit. Not in five years. Now. The disruption is already inside the classroom, and education is where it's hitting hardest.
Student AI use is sky-high. Professors are quietly conceding that the model often knows more than they do — and might teach it better, too.
Trying to exclude students from it is like trying to exclude students from a world powered by electricity. And even if you succeed, all you've really accomplished is removing them from the new world.

'I think if we continue to teach and evaluate students as if we were in a pre-AGI world, it's not going to work and it is going to lead to atrophy of learning how to think.' — Sam Altman, CEO, OpenAI, @ Stanford CS 153, 2026

The classroom has to become a place that does the things AI can't do for a student: build judgment, demand defense, reward original thinking under pressure. Debate, design thinking, entrepreneurship — these are the formats that survive contact with a machine that can write your essay for you.

When students debate AI rather than offload to it, their thinking explodes. Switch-side debating forces a student to genuinely understand the position they don't hold. That's a kind of comprehension no one-sided essay produces.
